card.hook: Picture a big golden dome, a 90-metre tower beside it, and nothing above them but bright sky. That's the view waiting for you in the marble courtyard, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon in the outer marble courtyard and face the central dome and the tallest minaret. They rise together above you, so you can get both in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the dome and tallest minaret together. Go to 0.5x for the long pools and the full façade, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome and minaret details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome and main minaret on one of the vertical lines, and let the marble courtyard fill the bottom third.
card.best_time: Go outside Fridays and public holidays, when the mosque is closed to visitors, and avoid prayer times. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone.
card.selfie_here: Try the marble paving in front of the main entrance arches, with the entrance behind you. Use the front camera, or switch to 0.5x if you want more of the arches in the shot, and check the framing when you arrive.
card.rules_and_safety: Leave worshippers out of your photos and ask permission before photographing anyone. Drones are typically restricted, so check the current rules on the day.
card.challenge: Catch the tall-and-short rhythm of the towers: the 90-metre main minaret and its shorter neighbours in one shot. Bonus points if the sky stays blue.
card.good_to_know: This is the largest mosque in Oman. It was inaugurated on 4 May 2001 and can hold up to 20,000 worshippers. It's built from about 270,000 tonnes of imported Indian sandstone.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon in the outer marble courtyard and face the central dome and the tallest minaret. They rise together above you, so you can get both in one frame.

card.hook: Locals call this market Al Dhalam, which means "darkness", and once you step into the lanes you'll see why: the stalls are so packed and the lanes so narrow that the sun barely gets in. The picture to grab first is outside, though, at the big domed gateway.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the souq's Corniche entrance, opposite the pedestrian traffic lights. Face the domed, arched gateway, so the Corniche and the harbour sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole gateway with the Corniche and harbour around it. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, then try 2x or 5x for arch details and stall goods (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, centre the gateway and keep your phone level so the arch doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds build up and while the light is nice on the gateway's detail. The entrance lanes get busy in the afternoon and evening, and busiest of all around Eid.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Corniche opposite the main entrance, by the pedestrian traffic lights, with the salmon-coloured domed pavilion behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the whole gate fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Corniche facing the entrance pavilion while you stand between them and the gate, so the whole gateway fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the souq are allowed, but ask before photographing vendors, as some don't want their displays photographed. Bring a bottle of water because the Oman heat is real, and check current opening hours before you go, since the hours online come from an old page.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the gateway with a few people walking through for scale, then dive inside and find a hanging lantern or a pile of colourful scarves to fill the frame.
card.good_to_know: Muttrah Souq is one of the oldest marketplaces in Oman, around two hundred years old, and it once did a great deal of trade in the age of sail. It was originally built from mud and palm leaves. The Muscat Municipality has since renovated and redecorated it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the souq's Corniche entrance, opposite the pedestrian traffic lights. Face the domed, arched gateway, so the Corniche and the harbour sit behind it.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: the Royal Opera House looks a bit shy from the street. It's a big building, but from far back it becomes a pale, glowing shape, and that's exactly why the view works.
card.stand_here: Stand on Al Kharijiyah Street, a stretch back from the building, and face the opera house. The street is a general area rather than one fixed spot, so pick a place by eye with a clear line to the building and safe pavement under your feet.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x and go up to 5x, depending on your phone, using the highest one that still looks sharp. At 1x the building shrinks to a tiny shape, and 0.5x won't help from here.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the picture a little darker so the lights don't burn out, and use night mode after dark.
card.best_time: Go at night, when the building is lit and stands out against the dark sky. In daylight the pale facade also reads nicely against the sky.
card.selfie_here: Head to the plaza in front and stand with the white facade behind you, ideally after dark when it's lit. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and let the building sit over your shoulder. For a daytime option, the courtyard with the arches behind you is a good midmorning stop for nice light and few people.
card.ask_someone: Stand a short way down Al Kharijiyah Street, away from the building, and ask your photographer to step back too so the whole facade fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your photos to the outside. Photography isn't allowed inside the auditorium during performances, and elsewhere inside only in designated public areas. The building has been closed on some holidays, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Frame the opera house through the date palms in the gardens, then see if you can spot the pink limestone against the white marble.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Opera House Muscat is Oman's main venue for opera, orchestral music and ballet. Sultan Qaboos ordered it built in 2001, and it opened on 12 October 2011 with a production of Turandot. It holds up to 1,100 people and also has a concert theatre, a cultural market and an art centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Al Kharijiyah Street, a stretch back from the building, and face the opera house. The street is a general area rather than one fixed spot, so pick a place by eye with a clear line to the building and safe pavement under your feet.

card.hook: Gold and blue columns march across the front in a perfect row, with one gate dead centre. Al Alam Palace is basically a symmetry puzzle that your phone can solve.
card.stand_here: Stand in the front forecourt, centred on the main wrought-iron gate, and face the palace. The phone icon on the map is right at the palace, so use it to find the front gate.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade with the columns and gate. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the gold-and-blue column details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gate, then drag the slider a touch darker so the sky stays blue and the gold doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early morning gives you softer light, and one guide suggests the hour around sunset. Midday is bright and the forecourt has little shade.
card.selfie_here: Head to the courtyard in front of the main gate and stand on the central marble walkway, close to the wrought-iron gate. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and tuck the palace in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the marble plaza facing the main gate while you stand in front of the gate, and ask them to step back along the central walkway if they can, since that brings the two forts into the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine from outside the gates but not beyond them, so follow any signs or instructions from security. Please don't photograph security staff. The courtyard has no shade, so bring a hat and sunscreen in the daytime.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line the gate up with the centre line so perfectly that the palace looks like it was drawn with a ruler.
card.good_to_know: Al Alam means "Palace of the Flag", and this is the Sultan of Oman's ceremonial palace, used for things like welcoming foreign dignitaries. Sultan Qaboos bin Said commissioned the current building, finished in 1972 after an earlier palace on the site was demolished in 1971. It sits between two old Portuguese-built forts, Al-Mirani and Al-Jalali.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the front forecourt, centred on the main wrought-iron gate, and face the palace. The phone icon on the map is right at the palace, so use it to find the front gate.

card.hook: Here's the odd thing about Muttrah Fort: the best photo of it is taken from the fort itself. Climb up and the harbour, the dhows and the souq rooftops are all laid out below you.
card.stand_here: Go up into Muttrah Fort and stand on the top ramparts, right by the battlements. Face out over the harbour and the bay, with the stone towers close beside you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x on the ramparts to squeeze in the harbour, the Corniche and the mountains. Switch to 1x for the towers and walls. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out dhows, souq rooftops and the Corniche below.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on a line with the harbour in the lower part of the picture, and let a battlement or tower frame one side.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset, when the stone and water catch golden light. The fort may close in the afternoon and may not be open at sunset, so check the opening hours on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the north-east tower: turn left after the gated entrance. One guide likes it for framing the fort's skyline, so use the front camera and see how much of the towers and battlements you can get around you. Selfie advice for this spot is thin, so take a few versions and pick your favourite.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Corniche promenade directly below the fort, facing up toward the walls and towers, while you stand in front of them with the fort behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The top of the fort is a ticketed viewpoint, and opening hours can vary, so check before you go. Wear comfortable shoes, because the paths and stairs up are steep.
card.challenge: Take the same view twice: once wide to show off the whole bay, then once zoomed in on a single dhow. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: Muttrah Fort stands on a hill above the Corniche in the Muttrah district of Muscat. Its height gives the widest panorama in the district. If you can't get in, the Muttrah Corniche is a good second choice, because from the promenade you can photograph the fort on its hill with boats and the harbour in front.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up into Muttrah Fort and stand on the top ramparts, right by the battlements. Face out over the harbour and the bay, with the stone towers close beside you.

card.hook: The best pictures at this weapons museum aren't of weapons. They're outside, where painted oryx sculptures stand in front of barasti huts and old Omani houses.
card.stand_here: Start on Al Saidiya Street in Old Muscat, at the stand-here point about 284 m south-west of the museum, and face north-east towards the museum. Take in the outer wall and entrance gate with the courtyard greenery peeking over the top, then head in for the village.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the huts and houses. Switch to zoom 0.5x in tight corners, and zoom 2x for the carved doors and the painted details on the oryx.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a shaded wall or doorway, then slide it a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the hut roofs.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. The light is softer and it's quieter, so you'll have more space for your shots.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Bait al Bagh entrance, the building with the painted oryxes, and use the front camera with the museum's face behind you. The model Omani village in the garden is another good spot, but no one says which way to face, so try a few angles.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum is ticketed and the garden is inside the paid grounds. Photos inside the buildings are restricted or banned according to several guides, and flash is limited almost everywhere, so keep it off and check the official site for photo rules first.
card.challenge: Find a hut doorway and use it as a frame, with an oryx sculpture peeking in from the side.
card.good_to_know: Bait Al Zubair is a museum in a restored Omani house on Al Saidiya Street. It's best known for its old weapons, including khanjar daggers, plus household objects and traditional costumes. Much of the collection comes from the owner's private collection.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start on Al Saidiya Street in Old Muscat, at the stand-here point about 284 m south-west of the museum, and face north-east towards the museum. Take in the outer wall and entrance gate with the courtyard greenery peeking over the top, then head in for the village.

card.hook: Big, plain buildings are sneaky: tilt your phone just a little and the walls start leaning like they're sharing a secret. The National Museum of Oman is a calm, wide subject, so it rewards a steady hand.
card.stand_here: Stand in Al Alam Square, across the square from the museum, and face the building. Walk a few steps left or right until it looks square to you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole frontage in, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. For a detail like an entrance or a strong wall line, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roofline or the base of the building with a horizontal line so the walls stay upright.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls than the middle of the day. After dusk, night mode can work if the building is lit, but rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the big open square in front of Al Alam Palace, standing in front of the main gate, so the museum ends up across the open space behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a little higher so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the National Museum of Oman, so keep yours in your bag if you go in. Photography rules inside can differ from outside, so ask at the entrance.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then one close-up of a single section, and see if you can make your two photos look like they're from different buildings.
card.good_to_know: The museum was set up by royal decree in 2013 and opened to the public on 30 July 2016. The building covers 13,700 square metres and was designed for the job. Inside are 14 permanent galleries and 5,466 objects, from maritime history to Islamic art.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Al Alam Square, across the square from the museum, and face the building. Walk a few steps left or right until it looks square to you.

card.hook: Sandy walls, a splash of harbour and rugged hills crowding in behind: Al-Mirani Fort gives you a layered picture even if you only stop for five minutes. Clear sky makes those stone towers glow.
card.stand_here: Stand in Al Alam Palace Gardens and face south. The fort's centre is about 59 m to the south, so you're at or near the edge of the fort and the whole building may not fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the fort sits in its harbour setting. Then try zoom 2x or more to pick out the towers and wall texture, and use 0.5x if it won't all fit.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the fort's horizon up with a horizontal grid line so the walls look level.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the walls than the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Pose against the outer stone walls and towers near the entrance, close to the parking area. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the towers rise up over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: In Al Alam Palace Gardens, where the fort and Al Jalali Fort are both in view, hand your phone to a passer-by and stand with the forts behind you while they shoot towards you.
card.rules_and_safety: Al Mirani Fort is reported to be an active military base and not open to the public, so plan to photograph it from outside. Wear comfortable shoes for the stairs and uneven areas.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then step forward and grab a tighter one. Bonus points if a boat drifts into the harbour behind the walls.
card.good_to_know: The fort was already here before the Portuguese arrived, and they rebuilt it in 1587. It's described as the first fort in Oman to use cannons. In 1552 an Ottoman force of 4 galleons, 25 galleys and 850 troops captured Muscat, and the fort was besieged for 18 days before it fell.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Al Alam Palace Gardens and face south. The fort's centre is about 59 m to the south, so you're at or near the edge of the fort and the whole building may not fit in one frame.

card.hook: From across the harbour, Al Jalali looks like one solid shape: walls and towers sitting on their rocky outcrop against the sea. Up close you'd never fit it all in, so enjoy the view from a distance.
card.stand_here: Stand at Al Mirani Fort (foot of the fort, on the opposite (western) side of the harbour) and face Al Jalali across the water. Stay in this one spot for both your wide and your close-up shots.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a wide shot with the fort sitting in its surroundings. It will look small from here, so then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the walls and towers. Skip 0.5x, which would shrink the fort even more.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the fort on one of the lines instead of dead centre, then tap the fort and drag the brightness down a little if the sky is washing out the walls.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is the best bet, when the softer light gives the walls more shape. Midday sun is harsher and flatter.
card.selfie_here: Try the plaza near Al Alam Palace on Al Alam Street in Old Muscat. Guides say the fort and Al Mirani frame the scene from there, though none promise the fort is right behind you, so check your screen first. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it so the fort peeks over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Across the harbour near Al Mirani Fort is where the whole fort shows against the sea, so ask a passer-by there to take your picture with it behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on public roads and out of restricted areas. Check the official site for visiting rules and access before you plan to go inside the fort.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up from the same spot, then see if friends can tell it's the same fort.
card.good_to_know: Al Mirani Fort is the twin fort across the harbour from Al Jalali, and the two make a pair. Al Jalali's full structure shows on its rocky outcrop against the sea from here. The official site has the fort's history and visiting rules.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Al Mirani Fort (foot of the fort, on the opposite (western) side of the harbour) and face Al Jalali across the water. Stay in this one spot for both your wide and your close-up shots.

card.hook: Picture a giant white incense burner on a hilltop, with the sea, the city and the mountains stacked up behind it. It's a simple shape, and the layers behind it do the showing off.
card.stand_here: Stand in Riyam Park, on the paths or the slightly raised areas below and around the monument, and look south-east to see the burner on its hilltop. Walk along until you get a clear line of sight, because trees and railings can block the view in some spots.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the sculpture, sea and city into one frame, then try 1x for a cleaner look. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to bring the burner closer without leaving the path.
card.make_it_pop: White can look washed out in strong sun, so tap the white sculpture and drag the brightness slider down a little until you can see its details.
card.best_time: Sunset or golden hour gives the sculpture softer colour. It's lit up at night too, so it makes a good second visit if you're staying nearby.
card.selfie_here: Try the rocky overlook beside the monument in Riyam Park, where visitors take photos with the sea and Mutrah spread out below. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and turn so the burner sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the whole monument in it, you could try Muscat Gate, where the burner can be seen across the view, and ask a passer-by to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the monument itself is restricted, so shoot from the park and please don't climb on it or damage it. Photography of the monument is allowed, and opening hours can vary, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Turn on your gridlines, put the burner on a vertical line, keep the horizon dead level, and see if you can do it in one go.
card.good_to_know: The Riyam Incense Burner stands on a hilltop in Riyam, a village in Muscat, in northeastern Oman. It looks out over the Mutrah waterfront and harbour. For a different view, Mutrah Corniche shows it small on its hill above the water, which suits a wide scene better than a close-up.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Riyam Park, on the paths or the slightly raised areas below and around the monument, and look south-east to see the burner on its hilltop. Walk along until you get a clear line of sight, because trees and railings can block the view in some spots.

card.hook: Most gates just let you through. This one lets you climb on top and look out over the sea and the rooftops of Mutrah. It's a great way to start a stroll into Old Muscat.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, on top of the Muscat Gate Museum on Al Saidiya Street. Face the sea and the Mutrah and old Muscat rooftops.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the gate edge and the whole townscape in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the Mutrah rooftops and the sea.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line so the sea stays level.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is more comfortable and gives softer light. The museum has been closed on some visits, so check opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the wide stairs leading up to the museum gate, where the Corniche is in view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the view fits behind you. The rooftop park up the small staircase is another good spot, but check on site how the gate frames up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing people, as is expected across Oman. Flash may be restricted inside the museum, so follow the posted signs or ask staff.
card.challenge: Catch the top edge of the gate in the corner of your shot, then see if the town and sea still look deeper.
card.good_to_know: The gate was built in 1995, and the museum inside opened in January 2001. It tells Oman's story from the Neolithic period to today, including how Muscat grew from a trading port into a modern capital. The old walled city's gates were once closed before sundown.
